figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: An illustration of a web interface generated by Gradio, which allows users to drag and drop their own images (left), and get predicted labels (right). Gradio can provide an interface wrapper around any machine learning model (InceptionNetv3 is shown in the example here). The web interface can be shared with others using the share link button (center top), and collaborators can provide feedback by flagging particular input samples (bottom right).
figures.headline: The generated web interface takes dragged images and returns predicted labels, with share and flag controls for collaborators.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: A diagram of the steps to share a machine learning model using Gradio. Steps: (a) The machine learning researcher defines the input and output interface types, and launches the interface either inline or in a new browser tab. (b) The interfaces launches, and optionally, a public link is created that allows remote collaborators to input their own data into the model. (c) The users of the interface can also manipulate the model in natural ways, such as cropping images or obscuring parts of the image. (d) All of the model computation is done by the host (i.e. the computer that called Gradio). The collaborator or user can interact with the model on their browser without local computation, and can provide real-time feedback (e.g. flagging incorrect answers) which is sent to the host.
figures.headline: Model computation stays on the host, while collaborators manipulate inputs and flag outputs from their own browser.

abstract: Accessibility is a major challenge of machine learning (ML). Typical ML models are built by specialists and require specialized hardware/software as well as ML experience to validate. This makes it challenging for non-technical collaborators and endpoint users (e.g. physicians) to easily provide feedback on model development and to gain trust in ML. The accessibility challenge also makes collaboration more difficult and limits the ML researcher’s exposure to realistic data and scenarios that occur in the wild. To improve accessibility and facilitate collaboration, we developed an open-source Python package, Gradio, which allows researchers to rapidly generate a visual interface for their ML models. Gradio makes accessing any ML model as easy as sharing a URL. Our development of Gradio is informed by interviews with a number of machine learning researchers who participate in interdisciplinary collaborations. Their feedback identified that Gradio should support a variety of interfaces and frameworks, allow for easy sharing of the interface, allow for input manipulation and interactive inference by the domain expert, as well as allow embedding the interface in iPython notebooks. We developed these features and carried out a case study to understand Gradio’s usefulness and usability in the setting of a machine learning collaboration between a researcher and a cardiologist.

sections.body: The introduction argues that domain experts without ML or coding skills cannot test models during development. This limits their feedback, exposure of models to real-world artifacts, and trust after deployment. The authors present Gradio, an open-source Python package that generates a web-based visual interface for a model. Collaborators can use the interface from a browser without installing software, and can give feedback on individual samples. The paper describes related work and limitations (Section 2), implementation (Section 3), a preliminary pilot study with an ML researcher and a clinical collaborator (Section 4), and next steps (Section 5).
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Domain experts usually cannot try ML models during development, so the authors built Gradio, a Python package that generates web interfaces.

sections.body:
Prior visual interfaces were tied either to a specific ML framework or to a specific application domain, which the interviewed researchers said made them unsuitable. The authors interviewed 12 ML researchers in interdisciplinary collaborations and derived four requirements:

- **R1:** support a variety of interfaces and frameworks, including Scikit-Learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch.
- **R2:** let developers easily create a shareable link without packaging the model or uploading it to a hosting server.
- **R3:** let domain experts manipulate inputs, such as cropping, occluding, or editing.
- **R4:** run and embed interfaces in Jupyter and Colab notebooks and websites.
sections.heading: Motivation
sections.headline: Interviews with 12 ML researchers yielded four design requirements for interfaces, sharing, input manipulation, and notebook embedding.

sections.body: A developer creates an `Interface` object with four required parameters: inputs, outputs, `model_type`, and the model itself. The `launch` function takes four boolean options: in-browser display, inline display, validation, and creating a share link. With a share link, the model keeps running on the host machine and an SSH tunnel passes data to it. Input data is encrypted before transfer. Collaborators need only a browser. Collaborators can flag outputs, which sends inputs, outputs, and a message to the researcher. The section states that user response time equals inference time plus network latency.
sections.heading: Implementation
sections.headline: Gradio wraps a trained model in an Interface object with four required parameters and shares it through a secure tunnel.

sections.body: The pilot involved one ML researcher and one cardiologist. Their pacemaker classifier had an area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.93. Setup took about 10 minutes. The cardiologist submitted an image, saw a correct pacemaker prediction, occluded the pacemaker, and saw the prediction switch to no pacemaker. Vertical flipping often significantly affected accuracy, and the cardiologist flagged those cases. The share button and notebook features went unused. The cardiologist requested pre-supplied images and saliency maps. The authors note the study covered one pair of users over a short time.
sections.heading: Pilot Study: Echocardiogram Classification
sections.headline: A single pilot pair found the shared link let a cardiologist probe a pacemaker classifier and flag failures.

sections.body: The authors argue that Gradio lowers the barrier for domain experts to take part in model development and test models in realistic settings. In the one case study, both the researcher and the cardiologist seemed relieved when the model worked, which the authors link to limited input manipulation and interaction. The authors state that the study covered one pair of users over a short time. Planned work includes more usability studies, quantitative measures of trust and user satisfaction, and features for saliency, tabular data, and bulk inputs.
sections.heading: Discussion & Next Steps
sections.headline: The authors expect the package to widen domain expert access, but a single short pair study cannot establish usefulness.
